catalog_quote: [p.6] /e/ is a voiced, high close, mid, unrounded vocoid; it has a lowered allophone which occurs immediately before /s/, nasals, /l/, and /r/ in closed syllables, and a shortened allophone which occurs in open syllables and in syllables in which the /e/ follows a glottal stop and preceeds a nasal that assimilates to the point of articulation of the following consonant. ... [p.7] A Tiruray syllable is made up of a vowel (V) which is the nucleus of a unit which may take stress. ... Thus the possible syllable patterns are CV and CVC. Most word bases consist of two syllables, but word bases occur with stems of one to five syllables; certain bases may be extended by affixation to as many as eight syllables. ... sources.citation: Blust, Robert. 1992. On speech strata in Tiruray. In Malcolm D. Ross (ed.), Papers in Austronesian Linguistics No. 2 (Pacific Linguistics A-82), 1-52. Canberra: ANU.
sources.quote: p. 18: 'Both Post (1966) and Schlegel (1971) recognise 16 consonant and 6 vowel phonemes in Tiruray ... Schlegel (p.7) states that primary stress "falls on the penult or antepenult of polysyllabic bases, except when the vowels of those syllables are shortened, in which case stress is on the ultima".' p. 6: 'Because none of the languages considered in this paper have retained stress contrasts, however, this feature of PPH reconstructions is ignored.' No synchronic examples; pp. 26-27 discuss only a historical correlation between PPH accent and initial-consonant loss.
sources.note: Restates Schlegel 1971: 7 for stress: the paper's one statement of Tiruray stress placement (p. 18) is a verbatim quotation of the catalog's own source, and its Tiruray data are taken from Post 1966 and Schlegel 1971; Blust's own remark (p. 6) is only that none of the languages compared has retained stress contrasts. Not an independent description of Tiruray stress.

sources.note: The only dedicated phonology of Tiruray and the primary analysis that Schlegel 1971's three-page key is 'adapted' from; our weight-hedged / full-vs-reduced-vowel coding rests on one unexemplified clause ('except when the vowels of those syllables are shortened') and the penult-vs-antepenult choice is unconditioned in the summary. Post should give stress-marked forms and the actual conditioning, and would settle whether Doty's 'unpredictable' framing or a reduced-vowel rule is right.
